title: CAP Theorem & PACELC Model
intro: The CAP theorem and PACELC framework define the fundamental trade-offs between consistency, availability, and latency across distributed storage nodes.
objectives: Prove why network partitions (P) are unavoidable physical realities.
Contrast CP systems (MongoDB, HBase, CockroachDB) with AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB).
Extend CAP using PACELC to evaluate latency vs consistency during normal non-partitioned operations.
body:
### Brewer's CAP Theorem
In a distributed network where communication delays or severed links (Partition $) can occur, a system can provide at most one of:
- **Consistency ($)**: Every read returns the most recent write or an error.
- **Availability ($)**: Every non-failing node returns a non-error response, but without guarantee of latest data.

Because network partitions cannot be prevented in physical networks, a distributed system must choose between **CP** (reject writes to preserve strict correctness) or **AP** (accept writes on isolated nodes, risking stale reads).

### The PACELC Theorem
Extends CAP by asking: **I**f there is a **P**artition, trade off **A**vailability vs **C**onsistency; **E**lse (normally), trade off **L**atency vs **C**onsistency.
- **PA/EL**: DynamoDB, Cassandra (prioritize availability and low latency).
- **PC/EC**: Spanner, CockroachDB (prioritize consistency at the expense of higher latency).
keyIdea: You cannot choose 'CA'. Physical networks will partition. The real decision is how you fail: degrade availability (CP) or serve stale reads (AP).

concepts.title: Split-Brain
concepts.body: When a network partition causes two groups of nodes to each elect their own leader, accepting conflicting writes.

concepts.title: Quorum Consensus
concepts.body: Requiring acknowledgments from a strict majority  = \lfloor N/2 floor + 1$ prevents split-brain leaders.

examples: Cassandra with Local Quorum vs Spanner TrueTime linearizable transactions.
